column4: After the battle turns, the ayah distinguishes among those who desire the worldly gain and those who desire the Hereafter; it directly stages the two choices the section weighs.
The warning names family, wealth, trade, and homes as loves that must not outrank God, His Messenger, and striving; it gives the section’s worldly preference a concrete list and a countermeasure.
The command not to fix one’s eyes on worldly adornment repeats the scene of 20:131, while its context contrasts patient company with a heedless follower of desire.

The ayah contrasts the one who seeks the Hereafter’s harvest and has it increased with the one who seeks the world’s harvest and receives only some of it; the harvest image joins the pasture scene to the choice of what lasts.
The passage addresses the Prophet’s tongue as he hastens to recite revelation, repeating the recitation setting of the source section’s assurance that he will not forget.
This ayah says God takes responsibility for gathering and reciting the revelation, directly paralleling the source section’s promise of recitation and preservation.
The next ayah instructs the Prophet to follow the recitation when it is recited, completing the same revelation scene.
The final ayah in this sequence assigns the explanation of the recitation to God, completing the passage that parallels the source section’s recitation and not-forgetting.
The ayah says people love the immediate life, an especially concise statement of the preference condemned by the source section.
The next ayah says they leave the Hereafter, completing the immediate-life preference as an explicit two-sided choice.

The deniers reduce existence to worldly life, death, and living again without resurrection; their denial of any enduring Hereafter is a sharp contrary boundary to the section’s preference for what lasts.
On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers are told they used up their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them; this makes the temporary enjoyment’s later cost explicit.
This ayah calls worldly life play and diversion, then links belief and mindfulness to reward; it names the passing side and the choice that points beyond it.
Rivalry in piling up possessions distracts people, a concrete form of choosing worldly accumulation over remembrance of what endures.
The next ayah says the rivalry lasts until visiting the graves, completing the accumulation scene with death as its limit.
The person who gathers and counts wealth supplies a concrete instance of worldly possession treated as the desired good.
The next ayah says the wealth collector thinks his wealth will make him last forever, a direct reversal of the source section’s distinction between passing wealth and true permanence.

The source section develops wealth as part of the worldly side; this ayah says people love wealth intensely, making that material pull concrete, though it does not use the source section’s root خ ي ر.
The ayah defines righteousness partly as giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and others; this is a specific choice to direct possessions away from self.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their love of the food, a concrete enactment of preferring others over oneself.
The next ayah says they seek neither repayment nor thanks, completing the selfless giving scene with its orientation toward God rather than worldly return.
A person gives up the self in seeking God’s approval, a specific reversal of keeping worldly benefit for oneself.
God’s purchase of believers’ lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden makes the choice of an enduring reward over worldly possession explicit.

This ayah names humiliation in worldly life and severe punishment in the Hereafter as the consequence of breaking the covenant; the next ayah describes that conduct as buying worldly life for the Hereafter.
The ayah distinguishes those seeking the reward of this world from those seeking the reward of the Hereafter, while allowing that the first may receive some worldly return.
An increase sought through usury does not increase with God, while charity seeking God’s face is multiplied; this distinguishes apparent material gain from value that endures.
The heavy scales mark the person whose good deeds outweigh, a concrete sorting of outcomes that parallels the section’s selection of what has true value.
The next ayah names that person’s pleasant life, completing the positive outcome of the heavy scales.
The ayah turns to the person whose scales are light, the contrary side of the sorting that the section imagines as leaving refuse behind.
The next ayah uses the term commonly rendered as “the abyss” for the light-scaled person, completing the consequence of the negative measure.
